title: Aponeurotic Ptosis: Clinical Masterclass
summary: A deep dive into the most common form of acquired blepharoptosis, characterized by the thinning, dehiscence, or disinsertion of the levator aponeurosis. This guide covers the essential diagnostics, surgical decision-making, and clinical nuances required for board-level mastery.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Aponeurotic ptosis (also known as involutional or senile ptosis) is an acquired drooping of the upper eyelid caused by the failure of the levator palpebrae superioris aponeurosis to transmit force to the tarsal plate. While usually age-related, it can be triggered by chronic inflammation, trauma, or intraocular surgery. Characteristically, the levator muscle function remains excellent, but the 'linkage' (the aponeurosis) is stretched or detached.

sections.title: The 'Classic' Clinical Tetrad
content: Variable Ptosis (often worse at the end of the day)
High or Absent Upper Eyelid Crease (Disinsertion point moves superiorly)
Good Levator Function (>12mm to 15mm excursions)
Thinning of the Upper Lid (Iris color may be visible through the skin)

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Ruling Out the Dangerous
Hering's Law of Equal Innervation
content: Always lift the more ptotic lid manually in clinic to check for 'drop' in the contralateral lid.
Ewald Hering's law: Bilateral levator muscles receive equal innervation.
Failure to identify subclinical ptosis results in post-operative 'asymmetry surprise'.

sections.title: The Phenylephrine Test
content: 1. Measure baseline MRD1 and Palpebral Fissure.
2. Instill 1 drop of 2.5% Phenylephrine into the superior fornix.
3. Wait 5-10 minutes for Müller muscle contraction.
4. Re-measure: If MRD1 normalizes, patient is a candidate for posterior-approach surgery (MMCR).

rows: Any ptosis, especially with excess skin (Dermatochalasis)
NOT for aponeurotic; only for poor LF (<4mm)

sections.title: Step-by-Step: External Levator Advancement
content: 1. Skin incision at the desired lid crease height.
2. Dissection through orbicularis to expose the orbital septum.
3. Opening the septum to identify pre-aponeurotic fat pads (the landmark for the aponeurosis).
4. Identification of the white, fibrous aponeurosis (often dehisced or thinned).
5. Advancing and suturing the aponeurosis to the mid-tarsal plate using 6-0 Silk or Vicryl.
6. Intraoperative adjustment: Patient sits up to confirm height and contour symmetry.
7. Skin closure with creation of a new lid crease (lid crease formed by skin-aponeurosis-skin sutures).

sections.title: Surgical Red Flags
content: Poor Bell's Phenomenon: High risk of exposure keratopathy.
Reduced Corneal Sensitivity: Post-op ulcer risk.
Dry Eye Syndrome: Ptosis repair can worsen symptoms.
Lagophthalmos: Avoid over-resection.

content.explanation: H: High lid crease, I: Involutional (Age), G: Good levator function, H: History of intraocular surgery/rubbing.

sections.title: Post-Operative Complications
content: Under-correction: The most common complication (approx 10-15%).
Over-correction: Leads to lagophthalmos and dry eye.
Eyelid Contour Peaking: Usually due to improper suture placement.
Eyelid Crease Asymmetry.
Retrobulbar Hemorrhage: Rare but vision-threatening emergency.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: The 'Iris Show' sign: If you see the iris through the skin, the aponeurosis is paper-thin or gone.
Always check for concurrent dermatochalasis; removing skin without fixing the ptosis makes the ptosis look worse.
In MMCR surgery, never include the tarsus in the clamp unless doing a Fasanella-Servat.
Warn patients with Hering's law drop that they may need bilateral surgery even if only one side looks bad initially.
